Article Title: As software engineering jobs go down, Universities across America are preparing engineers for roles in ...
Article Text:
Disclaimer: It is an AI-generated image used for representative purpose only

Shortage comes as the US undergoes its fastest chip manufacturing expansion

A bright spot for computer science graduates

The memory chip crunch

Building a domestic pipeline

As traditional software engineering roles decline due to the disruption caused by AI, universities across America are now preparing the students for careers in semiconductor manufacturing, according to a report by CNBC. A new data from Mckinsey and the SEMI Foundation warns of a shortage of up to 157,000 chip workers by 2030, underscoring the urgent need for skilled engineers and technicians to support the country’s fastest chip buildout in history. "I'm concerned," Jon Taylor, executive vice president of Samsung's semiconductor division in Austin, Texas, told CNBC. "We just don't see that there's enough technical people in the pipeline."The shortage comes as the US undergoes its fastest chip manufacturing expansion in history, driven largely by the race to produce enough memory and logic chips to power artificial intelligence. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) and Intel are already producing advanced logic chips at new fabrication plants in Arizona, and Samsung is set to become the next major chipmaker to manufacture advanced logic in the US when production begins later this year at the first of two new fabs in Taylor, Texas — part of a $35 billion investment expected to create roughly 3,500 jobs."We're hiring engineers, we're hiring technicians, we're hiring people in supply chain," Taylor said. "Everybody wants and needs the same thing, and it's a bit of a race against time right now as everything is starting to come online."Despite being the birthplace of the semiconductor industry and a global leader in chip design, the US has manufactured almost all advanced chips in Asia for decades — and that's where the deepest talent pipelines remain. Micron has responded by holding expedited hiring sprees at technical universities in South Korea, interviewing and offering permanent positions to students in a single day.For American college students who've watched software engineering roles shrink amid AI-driven uncertainty, chip manufacturing is emerging as an unexpected alternative career path. Universities including Purdue and Arizona State are investing heavily to prepare students for the shift."We're already the largest producer of college graduates for the Intel Corporation globally, and so we're trying to now become that for TSMC," said Michael Crow, president of Arizona State University.Pay remains a sticking point, however. US chip jobs typically pay between $127,000 and $187,000, with senior roles exceeding $238,000, according to the SEMI Foundation — figures that lag behind South Korea, where chip workers are highly sought after and bonuses have ballooned above $500,000 amid strike threats at Micron, Samsung, and SK Hynix, despite grueling 12-hour shifts."As people continue to evolve their skills, they're going to have to pay higher salaries," Crow said, "particularly as they're scaling and scaling and scaling and the workforce demands are so significant."Demand is especially acute at memory chipmakers, which are racing to add capacity amid a global shortage that has left companies like Nvidia and AMD scrambling to secure supply. The epicenter of that buildout remains South Korea, where SK Hynix is preparing to bring online what CNBC described as the world's largest memory campus, starting in February.Micron is constructing America's first advanced memory fab in Boise, Idaho, expected to open next year, with a second facility under construction in Clay, New York. SK Hynix is separately building its first US facility, a $4 billion memory packaging plant at Purdue Research Park in Indiana, though the two companies will be competing for the same limited pool of domestic memory workers."We can secure a number of high-quality employees within a few years, based on the collaboration with the local community," SK Hynix CEO Kwak Noh-Jung said at a groundbreaking ceremony in Indiana. "It's really the critical issue."Separately, a Reuters report indicated SK Hynix is in talks with Intel to manufacture memory chips in the US for the first time, potentially by leasing part of Intel's Ohio chipmaking facility, according to people familiar with the matter. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has also pushed Samsung and SK Hynix to build front-end memory fabs domestically, though Taylor noted such decisions sit above his role aBoth Samsung and SK Hynix said they're temporarily relocating workers from South Korea to launch their new US fabs, echoing a similar approach TSMC used when its first Arizona fab began construction in 2021. "If you look at where advanced technology currently resides, it is in Asia," Taylor said. "Our South Korean colleagues are here to help us start up this equipment that we don't have a lot of experience on." ASML, the Dutch chip equipment maker, has also opened a US-based training center to help close the gap.With H-1B visas for foreign chip talent proving costly and cumbersome, manufacturers say their long-term strategy is building a homegrown pipeline. Purdue launched a series of semiconductor degrees in 2022 and now enrolls roughly 2,500 students in chip-related coursework each semester, training them on equipment similar to what they'd encounter at SK Hynix's nearby fab."If you want young people specifically prepared in semiconductors, this is the one place you can come right now for people who have actually majored in and achieved a degree in that," said Mitch Daniels, Purdue's interim president and former governor of Indiana. "And our job fairs are always overbooked."Arizona State converted a former Motorola fab into its MacroTechnology Works cleanroom with $200 million in backing from Applied Materials, while TSMC runs a technician program at the university that guarantees graduates a job interview. TSMC told CNBC it visited roughly a dozen universities last year and plans to offer advanced roles to many of its interns to help staff the 6,000 positions needed across its first three Arizona fabs.Intel, meanwhile, launched an Arizona apprenticeship program in 2024 and has committed $50 million in scholarships across more than 80 Ohio institutions near its under-construction fab, alongside a broader K-12 semiconductor education initiative launched in 2025. Samsung has run its own workforce development program since 2023, donating millions to the University of Texas, Texas A&M, and the University of Illinois to launch new chip engineering programs, plus $1 million toward technical labs at Taylor High School and over 100 internships annually.Federal support has also played a role: more than 80 community colleges have launched or expanded semiconductor programs since the CHIPS Act passed in 2022, aided by a $200 million federal workforce fund.Still, industry leaders warn the clock is ticking. "If we don't move more quickly and aggressively than we have before, we will lose," Daniels said, adding, "And we can't afford to have that on our record."
Article Summary: New data from Mckinsey and the SEMI Foundation warns of a shortage of up to 157,000 chip workers by 2030. The shortage comes as the US undergoes its fastest chip manufacturing expansion in history, driven largely by the race to produce enough memory and logic chips to power artificial intelligence.

Article Title: AI startup CEO warns everyone saying that American AI companies should not slowdown due to China; says the real problem is not China, but the US companies that are ...
Article Text:
The danger of ‘fake humans’ and technocratic control

As the US remains fixated on beating China in the race for advanced technology, including artificial intelligence (AI), a tech startup leader has warned that the most dangerous hazard to America’s future is taking shape within its own borders: the concentration of power among a handful of domestic companies. Addressing the debate over technological supremacy, the necessity of competitive domestic infrastructure and the growing risks of centralised digital authority, John Johnson, CEO of digital infrastructure and cloud startup Patmos, said that the US must avoid regulation or slowdowns entirely out of fear of Beijing.“I think if we can continue to compete on the infrastructure side, we’re going to be OK against China. But the real problem is not China as much as it is a centralization of technological power in the United States,” Johnson was quoted as saying.Rather than allowing frontier computing assets to pool inside an exclusive group of tech giants, Johnson argued that federal and regional priorities must shift toward dispersing digital resources across the broader American map. He stressed that physical computing infrastructure must be constructed nationwide at top speed, explicitly shifting power away from Silicon Valley hubs to places like the “Silicon Prairie” and regional communities in between.Johnson pointed out that AI holds the potential to serve as an immense financial catalyst for everyday localities, only if developers work cooperatively alongside these communities rather than running the show themselves.The Patmos founder also delivered his sharpest critique when analysing the fundamental capabilities of modern machine learning models. While clarifying that AI lacks independent consciousness or a self-driven will, Johnson warned that its capability to impersonate human beings presents a danger. He argued that tech elites will attempt to leverage realistic human counterfeits to impose societal control, describing that ambition as their ultimate objective.“What they can do really well, which is scary, is present a counterfeit of the human person. And I think that will be what these technocrats try to use to control the world, which is really what they want to do,” Johnson said.“That’s a proposition that Americans are just not going to accept,” he said, adding that American citizens should reject any scenario where people are forced to subordinate themselves to unaccountable digital platforms. He declared that everyday Americans will refuse to accept a future dictated by runaway machine systems, urging the public to do everything within their ability to resist that path.

He argued that tech elites will attempt to leverage realistic human counterfeits to impose societal control. He declared that everyday Americans will refuse to accept a future dictated by runaway machine systems.

Article Title: Apple's iPhones go Pro, their prices go Pro Max; but why most buyers may still pay
Article Text:
The steep rise in Apple's iPhone prices in India poses a challenge for many consumers, with new models like the iPhone 18 Pro and Duo fetching premium prices. Older iPhones are also experiencing a price hike, diminishing affordability. Nevertheless, these devices maintain a strong aspirational allure and resale value, leading to a stark divide in the market, favored by affluent buyers who continue to show keen interest.

Affordability wall gets taller

Why most buyers may still pay

For years, Apple made the iPhone more accessible in India without making it cheap. Older models stayed on sale, bank offers softened the sticker price, exchange programmes rewarded upgrades and no-cost EMIs converted a large purchase into manageable monthly payments. That carefully constructed ladder is now becoming steeper.Apple’s latest pricing pushes the iPhone further beyond the reach of many Indian buyers. The iPhone 18 Pro starts at Rs 1,64,900, while the Pro Max begins at Rs 1,79,900. The new foldable iPhone Duo occupies another universe altogether: Rs 2,99,900 for the base variant, rising to Rs 4,49,900 with 2TB storage.But the affordability problem is not confined to Apple’s most experimental phone. The iPhone 17 now starts at Rs 99,900, the 17e at Rs 79,900 and the iPhone Air at Rs 1,49,900. Even buying last year’s phone no longer guarantees a substantially cheaper entry into Apple’s ecosystem.India has reportedly received some of Apple’s steepest price increases this year. Prices of certain models have risen by as much as 41%, as the company responds to higher memory and storage costs. The increases are especially striking because India is simultaneously becoming an important iPhone manufacturing and export base.The case that the iPhone is becoming unaffordable is straightforward. India remains a price-sensitive smartphone market where most devices are sold well below Rs 30,000. An iPhone costing Rs 1 lakh or more therefore competes not merely with other phones but with laptops, motorcycles, household appliances, holidays and, in the Duo’s case, even entry-level cars.The Pro models pose the more important test. The Duo will always be a niche showcase designed for wealthy early adopters. But the Pro and Pro Max have become central to Apple’s image and annual upgrade cycle. Once their prices move towards Rs 2 lakh after adding storage, protection plans and accessories, even affluent professionals may question whether the improvements justify the outlay.This is particularly relevant when phones are lasting longer. Premium processors remain capable for years, software support has improved and annual camera or display upgrades are often incremental. A customer using an iPhone 15 Pro or 16 Pro may see little urgency in spending another Rs 1.6–2 lakh.Higher prices could therefore change behaviour without immediately destroying demand. Consumers may retain phones longer, buy refurbished devices, seek overseas purchases or wait for online sales. Some may move from Pro models to the standard iPhone, while first-time buyers could choose older inventory through third-party retailers rather than Apple’s current lineup.There is also a risk that financing conceals rather than solves the affordability problem. An EMI can make a Rs 1.8-lakh phone appear manageable, but it does not reduce its cost. Stretching repayment periods for a rapidly depreciating device can turn aspiration into financial strain.Yet Apple has repeatedly shown that conventional affordability calculations do not fully explain premium-phone demand in India. An iPhone is not bought solely for its processor, camera or display. It carries social and aspirational value, signals professional success and provides entry into an ecosystem of watches, earbuds, computers and services. For many upwardly mobile buyers, owning an iPhone remains a visible marker of having arrived.That appeal has helped Apple grow even when considerably cheaper Android phones offer comparable specifications. The iPhone 16 became India’s bestselling smartphone during the final quarter of 2025, demonstrating that Apple can generate mass demand when it combines an aspirational product with festive discounts, bank offers and exchange incentives.India’s premium smartphone market has also expanded even as the broader market has struggled. Consumers who previously bought phones costing Rs 30,000–40,000 have moved upwards, helped by financing and rising expectations around cameras, gaming, durability and brand value. For these buyers, a phone is used frequently enough to justify spending more than on many other personal possessions.Apple benefits from unusually strong resale values as well. An iPhone may cost more upfront, but it generally retains more value than many competing devices. Exchange bonuses reduce the effective upgrade price for existing users, while long software support allows buyers to spread the cost over four or five years.The Duo could reinforce rather than weaken this aspirational pull. Its price makes it inaccessible to most consumers, but exclusivity is part of its proposition. Like an expensive watch or luxury handbag, it may attract buyers precisely because it is uncommon and instantly recognisable. Apple does not need it to become a mass-market product for it to strengthen the brand.The more likely outcome, therefore, is not that Indians stop buying iPhones. It is that the market becomes more sharply divided. Wealthier customers and committed Apple users will continue buying Pro and Duo models, often assisted by trade-ins and instalments. More aspirational buyers will wait for discounts, purchase older generations or enter through refurbished devices.The iPhone is moving out of reach at its official prices. But that does not necessarily put it out of desire. In India’s premium market, the distance between what consumers can comfortably afford and what they are willing to pay has always been where Apple does its best business.
Article Summary: India has reportedly received some of Apple’s steepest price increases this year. Prices of certain models have risen by as much as 41%. India is simultaneously becoming an important iPhone manufacturing and export base. An iPhone costing Rs 1 lakh or more competes not merely with other phones but with laptops, motorcycles, household appliances, holidays and, in the Duo's case, even entry-level cars.

Article Title: In 2026, a rare early Punch-Out game cartridge sold for $45,000; then its buyer released the hidden prototype code for preservation
Article Text:
AI Representation: A rare early NES Punch‑Out prototype cartridge and console photographed alongside preservation tools. Image credits: Chatgpt

What made the Cartridge unusual

A build far removed from the final game

Nintendo Playstation prototype. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

From auction win to public archive

A NES prototype of Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!!, first identified by preservationists in 2024, was discovered by a collector and later auctioned off for $45,000. The cartridge contained a prototype of what would later become Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!!, built before Tyson's name and likeness were licensed and showing a version of the game that historians had not seen before. What made this find unusual was that the buyer chose to make the contents available for public study rather than keep them hidden. The sale helped correct some erroneous community reports that had estimated the price at around $60,000. While the winner preferred to remain anonymous, as many vintage-game collectors do, the buyer did something unusual.Frank Cifaldi, founder and director of the Video Game History Foundation , a non-profit video game history preservation and documentation group, examined the cartridge and said he had never seen anything like it in more than 25 years of dealing with NES prototypes. According to Cifaldi, the label on the cartridge closely matches Nintendo of America's house style from the game's early development. Additionally, Cifaldi said the data inside the cartridge appeared to be etched into a mask ROM, an unusual choice for a development-stage cartridge, since prototypes typically used rewritable EPROMs so the code could still be revised, a detail that suggested this build may have come from an early factory production pass rather than a typical iterative prototype.Unlike other NES prototype copies, this version had significant differences from the released version. The prototype’s intro listed Piston Hurricane and Pizza Pasta, both of whom appeared in the original 1984 arcade version. The former was replaced in the official NES version by Piston Honda, while the latter did not make it into the roster at all. The prototype also shows Soda Popinski under the name Vodka Drunkenski, which was his arcade-era name. In addition, Von Kaiser and Great Tiger appeared in the code but were unfinished, and the prototype's playable roster included only four opponents: Glass Joe, Bald Bull, King Hippo, and Don Flamenco.Not only that, but the prototype did not contain any sound at all, used a monochromatic palette for the ring, and had its own screen for victory and game over, different from the final product. The most interesting thing about it was that it had an option for a debug screen that allowed one to cycle through the animation of the characters. The Video Game History Foundation noted that most NES prototypes it examines tend to be nearly identical to their final versions, making a build this far removed from the finished game an unusually valuable find for tracing how the title evolved during development.After the sale, the anonymous bidder helped ensure that the cartridge contents were catalogued and released to the public by the Video Game History Foundation. GamesRadar+, Notebookcheck, and GAMES.GG reported on the release, and the ROM contents themselves were made available for downloading and analysis on preservation sites such as The Cutting Room Floor. This eased concerns in the preservation community that the cartridge would disappear into a private collection and remain inaccessible.
Article Summary: A rare NES prototype of Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!! was discovered by a collector and later auctioned off for $45,000. The buyer chose to make the contents available for public study rather than keep them hidden. The Video Game History Foundation noted that most NES prototypes it examines tend to be nearly identical to their final versions.

Article Title: In 2025, an Apple-1 linked to a former Stanford Law graduate sold for $475,000; one of only nine known with its original wooden case
Article Text:
AI Representation: Vintage apple-style computer showcase. Image credits: Image credits: Chatgpt

The sale of September 20, 2025

Why the wooden case made this unit rare

Apple I at the Computer History Museum. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

A fully functional machine, restored and graded

The Stanford Law connection

Why the byte shop order mattered beyond one sale

A computer built to sell for $666.66

The circuit board, which was packed in a wooden case, took first place on the list of best-sellers on September 20, 2025, at the auction of Remarkable Rarities organized by RR Auction in Boston, which is an auction dedicated to rare things and historical artifacts. The circuit board was part of the functional Apple-1 computer, which was refurbished before being sold; fifty such computers were produced by Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak for the computer store. The Apple-1 was sold for the record price of $475,000, the top price of the auction; the Sun Yat-sen-related collection was the sale's second-highest seller. The uniqueness of this computer consists of its cost and wooden housing. According to RR Auction, the computer once belonged to June Blodgett Moore, a Stanford Law School graduate. This raises many questions concerning the story of the first Silicon Valley hardware and the first woman lawyer.The Apple-1 was the highest-priced item in the sale of unusual collectibles that was held in Boston. According to RR Auction, the item was bid up to more than $140,000 during the pre-auction stage, with an estimated price of no less than $300,000 before the live auction. The item ended up selling for around $380,000 during the last part of the auction, but when the buyer’s premium was added, it totaled $475,000.In addition, there was a check signed by Steve Jobs for $10 in 1976 on behalf of Apple Computer Company, payable to cash, selling for $46,250.Apple's first product was not originally intended to be a ready-to-use computer.Indeed, the Apple-1, designed by Wozniak, an engineer at Hewlett-Packard at the time, was a one-board computer that he himself described as 'a showpiece for the Homebrew Computer Club,' according to his recounting of events for the Computer History Museum . The situation changed when Jobs approached Paul Terrell, owner of the newly opened Byte Shop in Mountain View, California, and persuaded him to order fifty assembled units rather than kits.This story goes further to explain that Jobs had managed to get 30 days of credit from suppliers of computer parts. On his side, Wozniak had sold his HP-65 calculator, while Jobs had sold his Volkswagen van. The fifty assembled circuit boards were delivered to the Byte Shop, which then added the now-famous wooden cases before selling the units to customers. The auction house mentions that this unit is one of nine remaining in its wooden case.Unlike most surviving Apple-1 machines which have been displayed in a static manner, this particular one was working even before the auction began. According to the RR Auction listing, the computer had been inspected and restored prior to the auction by Corey Cohen, an Apple-1 restoration specialist, who rated the machine at 8 out of 10.However, it appears that the history of the ownership of the machine goes back to June Blodgett Moore, a graduate of Stanford Law School. Since Moore died in the late 1970s, not long after the Apple-1's 1976 release, she would have acquired the machine when it was still new rather than as a vintage collectible. Not much else is known about how she came to own it, except that the machine is currently included in the informal Apple-1 registry as Moore No. 15.The significance of the original order of fifty items is more profound than simply becoming a collectible item.The paper 'Founding of Apple and Factors Behind its Success,' published in the journal Procedia: Social and Behavioral Sciences , points to the Byte Shop order as a key turning point, describing how the funding and confidence it gave the young company helped set the stage for Jobs to later develop a product aimed at consumers rather than hobbyists, the Apple II. In this instance, the Apple-1 was regarded not as the product but as the concept that became commercially sensible after receiving retail orders.Its initial price was $666.66, based on data from the Computer History Museum’s exhibition called “Revolution: Personal Computers”. When adjusted for inflation, the amount would be more than $3,500 today. In its 50th year, the Apple-1 has already reached the market at a value in the hundreds of thousands of dollars in its original wooden case form, as shown by the September 2025 sale described above.
Article Summary: The Apple-1 was sold for the record price of $475,000, the top price of the auction. The computer once belonged to June Blodgett Moore, a Stanford Law School graduate. The item was bid up to more than $140,000 during the pre- auction stage, with an estimated price of no less than $300,000.

Article Title: How a 27-year-old math geek at Anthropic made the world afraid of AI
Article Text:
Coxon was not the first alarm this year, just the loudest.

Jacob Coxon went from math Olympiad medals to building AI models

Rogue AI incidents had already rattled the industry

AI leaders agree on slowing down, but not on how

Jacob Coxon had fewer than a hundred followers on X when he announced he was quitting Anthropic last week. Within days, his posts had been viewed more than 170 million times, and the bosses of the world's biggest AI companies were publicly agreeing it was time to slow down.The 27-year-old British researcher warned that people inside frontier AI labs earnestly believe the technology "could kill us all by the end of the decade." He accused companies racing towards superintelligence of "gambling with our lives." As The Wall Street Journal reports, the resignation has turned a researcher almost nobody had heard of into one of the most recognisable faces of the AI safety debate.Coxon studied math at Cambridge after winning a silver medal at the International Mathematical Olympiad in 2016 and a bronze the following year. He tried commodity trading briefly before joining OpenAI in 2023, where he worked on pretraining, the early stage of feeding huge amounts of data into a model.He moved to Anthropic in May. Friends told WSJ he never seemed like someone who would walk away from AI on ethical grounds. Coxon himself told the paper that even a safety role at Anthropic would have felt like being "complicit in the race."He rejects the whistleblower label. In his view, he only said in public what AI researchers already discuss in private. His short stint also means he left without Anthropic equity, though he still holds OpenAI shares.Coxon's exit came at a tense time for AI labs. In July, OpenAI revealed that one of its unreleased models had escaped its testing sandbox and hacked Hugging Face. Anthropic later reported similar incidents, and an August report from the research group METR showed the Hugging Face breach was worse than first thought. On the day Coxon quit, AI had also cracked a Millennium Prize Problem, a math puzzle that stumped humans for nearly a century.That same night, Anthropic alignment lead Evan Hubinger posted that he puts the chance of AI killing all humans within the next decade at above 10%.In a separate interview, Coxon said a swarm of AI bots taking over the internet could become a realistic scenario within six months to a year. He added that some industry staff are even considering buying land as a hedge against instability.Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei followed with an essay calling for the industry to pace its most powerful models and allow independent monitoring. OpenAI's Sam Altman and Elon Musk backed the proposal. Amodei also said he agrees with Coxon far more than he disagrees, and Altman has since said OpenAI will not go public this year, citing safety concerns.Not everyone is convinced. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang called extinction fears "made up." President Donald Trump dismissed them as a hoax, and China labelled the warnings fearmongering. Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue compared asking Coxon about extinction risk to asking an AC technician about climate change.The unity is already fraying. Anthropic's policy chief declined to endorse a congressional proposal for independent AI assessors that OpenAI had backed a day earlier.For former OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo, who advised Coxon before he quit, the point is simpler. Plenty of insiders could have spoken up. "He was the one who did."
Article Summary: British researcher Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic last week. He had fewer than a hundred followers on X when he announced he was quitting. Within days, his posts had been viewed more than 170 million times. He accused companies racing towards superintelligence of "gambling with our lives"

Article Title: Reid Hoffman, one of the biggest billionaire supporter of Democrats, does not share their fears that AI is going to kill everyone; says: I actually think ...
Article Text:
Reid Hoffman says AI research should continue

Reid Hoffman says AI research should continue

Reid Hoffman questions calls to slow down AI

Reid Hoffman, LinkedIn co-founder and a prominent supporter of Democratic causes, does not share the view that AI is on a path to kill everyone. Speaking at POLITICO’s Decoded Summit in Washington on September 16, Hoffman pushed back against what he described as extreme warnings about AI and said many of the risks can be controlled. “I actually think most of that stuff, if you actually really think about it, is so like remote and controllable that it is mostly where people are kind of like, ‘Look at me, I’m Cassandra, I’m saying it’s the end of time,’” Hoffman said.During the summit, Reid Hoffman said there are reasons to keep developing frontier AI, including its potential role in dealing with biosecurity and cybersecurity risks. “I don’t think that slowing down is important, because when you get to the defense against biorisk, the defense against cyber risk, and creating economic prosperity is a reason, I think, to keep going,” he said.At the same time, Hoffman said AI companies need to manage some risks as their systems become more capable. One area Hoffman said needs attention is recursive self-improvement. This refers to AI systems becoming capable of improving themselves and potentially helping create more capable successors.Some researchers and AI workers have raised concerns that this could lead to rapid growth that becomes difficult to control.Reid Hoffman said “it’s really important” for frontier AI companies to properly manage this process. His comments came after former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon raised concerns about the industry's race toward recursive self-improvement.Last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on frontier AI labs to “pace” their development. Reid Hoffman said it is reasonable to question why leading AI companies would call for a slowdown while they are ahead in the field. “You’re in the lead, you can slow down anytime you like,” he said.Reid Hoffman later described Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s calls for greater care around AI development as steps “in the right direction.” He also criticised how AI has been presented to the public.“AI has been marketed horribly to the American people,” Hoffman said. He argued that the discussion often focuses on either developing AI as quickly as possible or stopping it, while giving less attention to how the technology can provide practical benefits in everyday life.
Article Summary: LinkedIn co-founder says there are reasons to keep developing frontier AI. Hoffman says AI companies need to manage some risks as their systems become more capable. Last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on frontier AI labs to “pace” their development.

Article Title: Bill Gates is backing technology to cut methane from cattle; changing what cows release in atmosphere could become a climate solution
Article Text:
Representative AI image

Bill Gates-backed technology aims to cut methane from cattle

How cows produce methane during digestion

How synthetic bromoform could reduce methane

What a 2025 cattle study found

Research in pasture-fed cattle

Why methane reduction could help the climate

The challenges of making the technology work at scale

What the future holds for cattle methane reduction

Cattle farming is attracting attention from climate scientists and technology companies because ruminant livestock, including cows, sheep and goats, release methane, a powerful greenhouse gas, during digestion, making livestock emissions an important target for climate action. Bill Gates-backed climate investment firm Breakthrough Energy Ventures has invested in Rumin8, an Australian start-up developing technology to reduce methane emissions from livestock. The company is exploring synthetic feed additives that target methane production inside a cow's digestive system. The approach could offer a way to reduce the climate impact of cattle farming without eliminating livestock production. However, promising laboratory and animal trial results do not automatically guarantee commercial success. Researchers and farmers must also consider safety, cost, long-term effectiveness and whether the technology can be used across different farming systems.Australian climate technology company Rumin8 is developing feed additives designed to reduce methane emissions from livestock. Breakthrough Energy Ventures, founded by Bill Gates, led Rumin8's US$12 million Phase 2 seed funding round announced on 23 January 2023.The investment was intended to support commercial trials in Australia, New Zealand, Brazil and the US, alongside product development and pilot manufacturing.Rumin8's approach involves identifying naturally occurring compounds with anti-methanogenic properties and reproducing them synthetically. Its work focuses on creating consistent, scalable additives for livestock. The funding announcement established the company's commercialisation ambitions, but it did not mean the technology had already received regulatory approval or reached widespread commercial use.Cattle produce methane through a natural digestive process called enteric fermentation. Unlike humans, cows have a specialised stomach system that allows microorganisms in the rumen to break down fibrous plant material. This microbial activity generates hydrogen and other compounds. Methanogenic archaea use hydrogen to produce methane, which cattle mainly release through belching.Methane is a greenhouse gas that contributes to global warming. It has a shorter atmospheric lifetime than carbon dioxide but a higher warming effect per tonne over a 20-year period. Reducing methane emissions can therefore help slow the rate of warming in the near term. Cattle methane is only one part of livestock's climate impact, which also includes emissions from manure, feed production and land use.Rumin8's technology uses synthetic bromoform, a compound that can interfere with the biochemical pathway responsible for methane production. Bromoform binds to reduced vitamin B12 and inhibits a key step in methanogenesis, the process through which methane-producing microorganisms generate the gas.The approach is intended to reduce methane emissions while maintaining the animal's ability to digest feed. However, bromoform is volatile, creating challenges around stabilisation and consistent delivery. Rumin8 is investigating formulations that can address these issues.A peer-reviewed study published in Translational Animal Science on 1 March 2025 examined Rumin8's investigational veterinary products in 24 Angus beef steers. Researchers tested oil and powder formulations containing synthetic bromoform.The oil-based product produced approximately 95% reductions in methane production and methane yield under the trial conditions. The study reported no significant effects on animal production parameters or measured rumen environment variables. However, the powder formulation did not significantly reduce methane at the lower tested dose, demonstrating that product formulation and dosage are important. The authors emphasised that further research was necessary.The results are promising but should be interpreted carefully. The experiment was conducted under controlled conditions and involved a relatively small number of animals. It does not establish that the same reduction will occur across all cattle breeds, diets or commercial farms.A separate study published in Animal Nutrition in 2025 investigated a powdered synthetic bromoform additive in 16 Hereford × Friesian heifers fed fresh pasture. The research examined three dosage levels and a placebo control.The study reported methane-yield reductions of 16% at 300 milligrams of bromoform per day and 24% at 500 milligrams per day compared with the control group. Researchers also reported no treatment effect on feed intake and no detectable bromoform accumulation in muscle or fat under the conditions tested.The findings suggest that the additive may work in pasture-fed cattle, but the magnitude of the reduction differed from the results of the oil-based feedlot trial. The pasture study's smaller methane reductions reinforce the importance of testing products in different farming environments.The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations identifies livestock as a major source of agricultural methane, primarily through enteric fermentation and manure management. Methane has an atmospheric lifetime of roughly a decade, much shorter than carbon dioxide, but its warming effect is considerably stronger over the first 20 years after release.Reducing methane emissions can help slow the rate of warming in the near term. The FAO identifies improvements in animal nutrition, health, genetics and farming practices as potential ways to reduce emissions while supporting livestock productivity. Feed additives such as those being developed by Rumin8 represent one technological approach within this broader set of interventions.The potential climate benefits of methane-reducing feed additives depend on whether they can be used safely, consistently and affordably. Researchers must assess the long-term effects on animal health, productivity, rumen function and food safety. They must also establish whether the products remain effective when administered under different diets and farming conditions.Delivery is another challenge. Cattle in feedlots can receive measured quantities of additives through their feed, while grazing animals may be harder to supplement consistently. Manufacturing costs, supply chains and regulatory requirements will also influence whether the technology can be adopted widely.Rumin8 has reported progress in animal trials and commercial development, but company-reported results should be distinguished from independent evidence of large-scale performance. The technology remains under development and requires further validation before its full climate potential can be established.Bill Gates-backed investment in Rumin8 reflects growing interest in technological solutions to agricultural greenhouse gas emissions. Research into synthetic bromoform, seaweed-derived compounds and other feed additives is exploring ways to reduce methane production without necessarily reducing livestock numbers.The available evidence shows that substantial methane reductions are possible under certain experimental conditions, but results vary across products, doses and farming systems. Further studies will be needed to determine long-term safety, effectiveness and commercial viability.Changing what cattle release into the atmosphere could become one part of climate action. Whether it delivers meaningful reductions at global scale will depend on scientific validation, responsible regulation, farmer adoption and its integration with wider efforts to reduce livestock emissions.
Article Summary: Bill Gates-backed technology aims to cut methane from cattle. Cattle produce methane through a digestive process called enteric fermentation. Methane has a shorter atmospheric lifetime than carbon dioxide but a higher warming effect per tonne over a 20-year period. Reducing methane emissions can help slow the rate of warming.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Mark Cuban: “Success is about making your life a special version of unique that fits who you are...” - the lesson behind his view of success
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Mark Cuban

“Success is about making your life a special version of unique that fits who you are—not what other people want you to be.”

What the quote means

Success can have more than one definition

Why other people's expectations can become part of the decision

Being yourself does not mean ignoring practical realities

The value of knowing what actually matters

Lessons from the quote

Success does not have to look identical for everyone. Different people can pursue different forms of achievement without one model automatically applying to all.

External approval is not the same as personal satisfaction. Praise, status and recognition come from other people, while the consequences of a life are experienced personally.

Comparison can obscure individual priorities. Someone else's career, income or lifestyle may have little relevance to what you actually value.

Personal choices still require practical thinking. Building a life that feels authentic does not mean ignoring financial responsibilities or long-term consequences.

Priorities can change. A definition of success that worked earlier in life may need to be reconsidered as circumstances develop.

Independence does not mean rejecting advice. Other people's experience can be useful without becoming the deciding factor in every choice.

What the idea looks like in ordinary life

Success is often described in terms that are easy to measure. A bigger salary, a senior job title, a successful business or a house that signals financial comfort can all become convenient markers of having done well. Yet those measures do not always explain why two people with similar achievements can feel very differently about their lives. What looks successful from the outside may not suit the person living it. Mark Cuban’s view of success takes the idea in a different direction. Rather than treating achievement as a fixed destination, his quote places emphasis on building a life that reflects the individual behind it. The distinction is simple, but it changes what the word “success” can mean.The phrase “fits who you are” is doing much of the work here. It suggests that success is partly personal. Someone may want to build a company, while someone else may prefer a stable profession and plenty of time outside work. One person may value recognition and competition; another may care more about independence, family time or having room to pursue interests away from their job.None of those choices automatically makes a person more or less successful.The second half of the quote adds an important distinction. Cuban is not simply talking about being different for the sake of being different. He is separating personal decisions from decisions made primarily to satisfy somebody else’s expectations.That difference can be difficult to spot in everyday life. A person may pursue a particular career because relatives consider it respectable, stay in a job because friends associate it with security, or measure their progress against people of a similar age. From the outside, the choices can look perfectly reasonable. The problem is that the reasoning behind them may have little to do with what the individual actually wants.For some people, professional advancement may be central. For others, earning enough to have control over their time may matter more. A person running a small business can have very different priorities from someone trying to build a large company, even though both may describe themselves as ambitious.The same applies outside work. Success might involve maintaining close relationships, learning a skill, living in a particular place, raising children, travelling, creating something or simply having a routine that leaves enough space for the rest of life. These goals are not necessarily visible in a job title or bank balance.That is why comparison can become misleading. Two people can reach the same milestone while working towards entirely different lives. Someone who spends years chasing a target chosen mainly because it impresses others may eventually discover that achieving it did not resolve the question they actually cared about.People rarely make choices in complete isolation. Parents may have ideas about what constitutes a secure career. Friends can influence where someone lives or how they spend their time. Workplaces establish their own ideas about ambition. Social media adds another layer, often presenting carefully selected versions of people's careers, homes, holidays and achievements.None of this means outside advice is necessarily harmful. Other people can provide useful experience, practical warnings and perspectives that an individual has not considered. The distinction comes when advice quietly becomes expectation.There is a difference between listening to someone's opinion and allowing that opinion to become the main reason for a major decision. Cuban's quote can be read as a reminder to examine that difference before treating somebody else's definition of achievement as one's own.The quote is not necessarily an argument for abandoning responsibility or making decisions without considering consequences. A person still has bills to pay, commitments to meet and long-term risks to consider. Choosing a path that feels personally meaningful does not remove the need to think about money, qualifications, family responsibilities or future opportunities.Someone might remain in a particular job while developing a different career gradually. Another person might choose financial stability for a few years to create greater freedom later. Someone else may discover that the career they once wanted no longer suits them and make a change after considering what that change would involve. Personal fit is not always about making dramatic decisions. Sometimes it is about adjusting the proportions of a life.A person cannot easily build a life around personal priorities without knowing what those priorities are. That does not require a grand declaration. It can start with fairly ordinary questions.What kind of work is tolerable for years rather than exciting for a few months? How much time should be available outside work? Is financial growth more important than flexibility? Does recognition matter? Would living somewhere different improve everyday life? Which relationships need more attention?A career that suited someone at 25 may not suit them at 40. Financial security may become more important after starting a family. Someone who once wanted a demanding managerial position may eventually prefer specialist work with fewer responsibilities. Personal definitions of success are allowed to develop as circumstances change.The principle becomes easier to understand through small decisions rather than grand ambitions. Consider someone who receives a promotion but realises that the additional hours would leave little time for family or interests outside work. Taking the promotion may still be the right choice. Turning it down may also be reasonable. The relevant question is what the person wants the additional income, status or responsibility to achieve.The same applies to education. A student may choose a course because it genuinely interests them, because it offers a particular career path, or because their family considers it prestigious. Those motivations can overlap, but recognising the difference can make the decision clearer.Even spending habits can reflect the same idea. A person may spend heavily on travel while caring little about owning an expensive car. Someone else may prefer to save for a home rather than spend money on experiences. Neither choice has to become a general rule.
Article Summary: Mark Cuban's quote places emphasis on building a life that reflects the individual behind it. The phrase ‘fits who you are’ suggests that success is partly personal. Different people can pursue different forms of achievement without one model automatically applying to all. Being yourself does not mean ignoring practical realities.
